questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to leave Europe (going to another continent), I wanted to go to an English-speaking country (to perfect my English). And I felt like that America gets all attention, so I wanted to see what Canada is like. Also because this country has such a good reputation throughout the world.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was simply fantastic, even though there was a lockdown in Ontario the 1st month of my exchange. But from mid-February and to the end of the exchange everything was just amazing.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The process of going on exchange is extensive, long and thorough. Especially catalyzed by covid. Once you are enrolled in McMaster, there is still amounts of bureaucracy to do. But the good thing, though, is that the people from the university are very helpful, quick-responding on mail and seem to sincerely wanting to help you.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Not really anything. You get a mail and access-link to their platform 'Mosaic' that can be said to correspond to KUnet. And then you have 'Avenue2learn' that corresponds to Absalon. I found it pretty easy to navigate around. Simplistic design with all the needed information and courses etc easily accessible. It can be convient to check out this before arriving though, so that you're familiar with the portals already.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I think this was pretty sufficient. And I think in circumstances without covid dominating every bureaucratic procedure, then the process of getting settled into McMaster should not be too bad actually.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: This was not very easy. There is a little selection of houses, and especially if you are only looking for a 4-month (trimester) lease. But advice is to access all the Facebook-groups. Most people I know found their place through the platforms here. Leases will appear now and then so you have to check in these groups regularly over a period of time and you should have a fair shout of at least getting in touch with some tenants.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Quality in houses can vary extremely much. My room was in such bad shape that I would not recommend that very room to anyone else. It was significantly cheaper than on campus and in Canadian universities as a whole.
Make sure to get a toor of your potential house! (at least virtual)

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Generally the quality of houses is better in Copenhagen than Hamilton in my opinion. 
Also I lived in the downtown area which is not too nice. When looking for houses I highly recommend to look in the Westdale-area where the university is located at, which also is the cosiest & nicest place of town. People living here e.g., rarely go to downtown. I had to commute around 35-40 min from home to university.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
There is one major obstacle here. To be approved into the courses you want to pick at McMaster, you have to provide some sort of proof that you meet their prerequisites (i.e., certain courses to be passed to enroll in other courses). So basically you have to check course requirements in course outlines from McMaster (this information is easily accessible though), and then send a mail to the course-responsible at McMaster providing proof that you fulfill the requirements, so they will allow you to enroll in the courses you want in their portal.

Here it is a good idea to be proactive and get this done not too late so that you make sure the courses are not full before you are able to enroll. (... but no matter what there should be plenty of courses available even until course enrollment deadline.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: McMaster course platform is decent. And the coordinators were responding quickly, so there were no issues here.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the courses I wanted. :) They even helped me with one of them that was actually full

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: As aforementioned it can be beneficial to start this process early on. Helps relieving the stress getting as much stuff done as early possible.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I found the courses interesting. It was a big experience to try the academical approach in North America that actually is a bit different than what we in Cph are used to.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
A took a POLSCI course that was significantly easier than all the ECON-courses I've had back in CPH. Economics of Labour Market Issues was also significantly easier than what you would expect at CPH. These two course were Level 2
The level 3 courses Economic Development and Game Theory were harder.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Here is midterms through all semester. This implies you have to study all semester as these tests have a significant impact on your grade. They counted up to 30% for me. But if you study for these and do relatively well you end up having not too much pressure regarding the final exams. You have more time, the questions are easier (can be just describing economic terminology) than what is the case in CPH, so I've tried leaving more than 1hr early in these tests and still be getting good grades.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Introduction to Game Theory
Economic Development
Economics of Labor-Market Issues
Globalization and the State

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Game Theory corresponds to Mikro III at KU so if you want to get this one done just having to pass, then pick it here.
Economic Development was more challenging and similar to the courses at KU. If you do not want academical challenges then you should pick as many level 2 courses as possible. My intention of going to Canada was for traveling and experiences and not  really academically purposes, so I did not care about getting academically challenged.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Food is surprisingly expensive in Canada. And also the quality is not good (in my opinion!). Unhealthy food is cheap, good food expensive. Traveling inside Canada is also expensive. If you check airlines like Swoop, Flair, and Westjet you can get some pretty cheap tickets to Montreal, Vancouver etc. Public transport outside big cities is non-existent!

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: I did not buy any of the books... Through McMaster you get free access to the bus system in Hamilton, which is decent, and this saves a lot of money.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Because of covid this was basically closed. I guess post-covid there would be plenty of fun clubs.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I did a trip with the outdoor club to a nationalpark 4hrs north of Toronto. This was expensive but such a fantastic experience and a nice opportunity to talk to some Canadian people.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Try to join some stuff if you are on exchange with the intention of meeting new people. This is by far the best approach. I enjoyed it very much and if you can manage to get some relations in the start of the exchange this will potentially give you the possibility to have so incredibly much fun.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Hangout in Hamilton. Plenty of places, go to Toronto. Travel around Canada. Even America is easily accessible. Take advantage of the fact that you are in North America, living here! Do all the stuff that you are not  able to do at home :-) Because 4 months is actually a short time and you will have to go back to DK quicker than you realise. And then you do not  want to regret that you said no to opportunities over in Canada!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: No problems here. You can easily sense that Canada and Denmark are both some of the very best countries in the world. It is not  hard at all acclimatizing.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Go to social clubs, say yes to stuff, be open to hangout. Try to not only sticking to hanging out with the other Danish people.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Canadians do not really go out to the bars for parties. Bars close at 1am in weekends already and lots of clubs close at 2am. So instead they do homeparties in their 'frat-houses' so social life here depends a lot of having a network through which you are invited to parties. Here I prefer Denmark where people go out for the fun stuff and in evenings.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: It is true that Canadians are kind. (sometimes even a bit too much, haha...) Everything is in order in this country. You have such close access to Toronto, so go and see NHL, NBA, MLB!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Exchange is expensive. That is the way it is. There is no way around! Everyone spends more than they intend to. But the day you are going back to Cph you would not give away any of these memories you create for a bunch of money. I guarantee that! 
2. Be open-minded. Talk to other people! Not only other Danes. (Because you can do that at home all the time...) You have such interesting conversations and you get sooo much perspective
3. Take advantage of the fact your grades don't matter. It does not matter if you get A+ or D-. The only person it matters for is yourself. So this is a great opportunity to relax a bit regarding school and have fun instead, especially as you do not have a job in Canada as well.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Send mails to people from McMaster and KU if you have doubts about anything. They are helpful
And the first month abroad can feel a bit weird because it is so new. But as the first month passes by you get used to it. It is a pretty cool feeling to realize that you are able to cope on your own. You really develop personally in a way you would not  be able to back home at a regular semester in Copenhagen.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Everything. It is not possible to point out a single thing. Though all the relations you create are such blessings.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: To balance travel, fun, parties, school properly. You want to do everything, but you only have 24 hours in a day ;-) But do not be sad about what you did not do and rather appreciate what you have done.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Make up your mind regarding what you ambition of this exchange is. I knew I was here for the North American experience, the fun and traveling. I even designed my schedule such that I was free every Friday. And I do not regret it the least!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
